definition: The force of attraction between atoms or ions that holds them together in a compound.
clues: This is a concept in chemistry
It holds atoms or ions together
It can be ionic, covalent or metallic
The electrostatic attraction that joins atoms or ions — can be ionic (transfer), covalent (sharing) or metallic

definition: The strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions formed when electrons are transferred from a metal to a non-metal.
clues: This is a type of chemical bond
It forms between a metal and a non-metal
Electrons are transferred in this process
The attraction between positive and negative ions — formed when a metal transfers electrons to a non-metal

definition: A bond formed when two atoms share a pair of electrons. Occurs between non-metal atoms.
clues: This is a type of chemical bond
It forms between non-metal atoms
Electrons are shared in this process
A bond formed by two non-metal atoms sharing a pair of electrons — the shared pair is attracted to both nuclei

definition: The attraction between a lattice of positive metal ions and a sea of delocalised electrons. Explains the conductivity and malleability of metals.
clues: This is a type of chemical bond found in metals
It involves delocalised electrons
It explains why metals conduct electricity
The force of attraction between positive metal ions and a sea of free electrons — explains conductivity and malleability

definition: A compound formed by ionic bonding, consisting of a lattice of oppositely charged ions held together by strong electrostatic forces.
clues: This is a type of compound
It forms between a metal and a non-metal
It has a giant lattice structure
A compound made of ions in a regular lattice — high melting point, conducts electricity when dissolved or molten

definition: The regular 3D arrangement of oppositely charged ions in an ionic compound. Ions are held together by strong electrostatic forces in all directions.
clues: This is a type of structure in ionic compounds
It is a regular, repeating 3D arrangement
It is held together by strong electrostatic forces
A repeating 3D structure of positive and negative ions — the strong forces in all directions give high melting points

definition: A structure made of small molecules held together by weak intermolecular forces. Examples: water, carbon dioxide, hydrogen. Low melting points.
clues: This is a type of structure with a low melting point
It is made of small molecules
The forces between molecules are weak
Small molecules held by weak intermolecular forces — low melting/boiling points and does not conduct electricity

definition: A large structure where many atoms are joined by covalent bonds in a giant lattice. Examples: diamond, graphite, silicon dioxide. Very high melting points.
clues: This is a type of covalent structure with a very high melting point
Many atoms are joined by covalent bonds
Diamond and graphite are examples
A vast network of atoms joined by covalent bonds — extremely high melting points due to many strong bonds

definition: A form of carbon with a giant covalent structure where each carbon atom is bonded to four others in a tetrahedral arrangement. Very hard, does not conduct electricity.
clues: This is a form of carbon
It has a giant covalent structure
It is the hardest natural substance
Each carbon bonded to four others in a tetrahedral lattice — extremely hard, very high melting point, does not conduct electricity

definition: A form of carbon where carbon atoms are arranged in layers of hexagonal rings. Layers can slide over each other and delocalised electrons allow it to conduct electricity.
clues: This is a form of carbon
It has layers that can slide over each other
It conducts electricity unlike other giant covalent structures
Flat hexagonal layers of carbon atoms — layers slide over each other (lubricant) and delocalised electrons allow conductivity

definition: A single layer of graphite — one atom thick sheet of carbon atoms arranged in hexagons. Extremely strong and conducts electricity.
clues: This is a form of carbon only one atom thick
It is a single layer of a more familiar carbon form
It is extremely strong for its size
A single layer of carbon atoms in hexagons — incredibly strong, flexible and electrically conductive

definition: A molecule consisting of carbon atoms arranged in hollow spheres, tubes or other shapes. Buckminsterfullerene (C₆₀) is the most well-known example.
clues: This is a form of carbon
It can form a hollow ball or tube shape
Buckminsterfullerene (C₆₀) is the most famous example
Carbon atoms arranged in hollow spheres or tubes — C₆₀ looks like a football and has potential uses in drug delivery

definition: A cylindrical fullerene made of carbon atoms rolled into a tube. Very strong, conducts electricity and has potential uses in electronics and materials.
clues: This is a form of carbon shaped like a tiny hollow tube
It is made of a rolled sheet of a single carbon layer
It is extremely strong and conducts electricity
A rolled graphene sheet forming a cylinder — incredibly strong, conductive, used in nanotechnology and electronics

definition: An electron that is not associated with a specific atom or bond and is free to move through a structure. Responsible for electrical conductivity in metals and graphite.
clues: This is a type of electron
It is free to move through a substance
It is found in metals and graphite
An electron not held by any particular atom — free to flow, which is why metals and graphite conduct electricity

definition: A lattice of positive metal ions surrounded by a sea of delocalised electrons. The mobile electrons explain conductivity, and the lattice explains malleability.
clues: This is a type of structure found in metals
It has a sea of free electrons
It explains why metals are conductive and malleable
Positive metal ions in a regular lattice surrounded by delocalised electrons — explains conductivity, malleability and high melting points

definition: A weak force of attraction between molecules. Responsible for the physical properties (melting and boiling points) of simple molecular substances.
clues: This is a type of force that acts between molecules
It is weaker than a covalent bond
It determines the melting point of molecular substances
A weak attractive force between separate molecules — stronger forces mean higher melting and boiling points

definition: A large molecule made from many small repeating units (monomers) joined together by covalent bonds.
clues: This is a type of very large molecule
It is made from many small repeating units
Polythene and nylon are examples
A long chain molecule made by joining many monomers together — e.g. poly(ethene), nylon, PVC

definition: A small molecule that can be joined with many others of the same type to form a polymer.
clues: This is a small molecule that can join with many others
Many of them link to form a larger molecule
Ethene is an example
A small repeating unit that links with others in polymerisation — e.g. ethene monomers form poly(ethene)

definition: A reaction where many monomers containing a double bond join together to form a polymer, with no other products formed.
clues: This is a type of polymerisation reaction
It involves monomers with double bonds
No other products are formed besides the polymer
Alkene monomers open their C=C double bonds and link together — the only product is the long-chain polymer

definition: A polymer that softens when heated and can be remoulded. Made of polymer chains with weak intermolecular forces between them.
clues: This is a type of polymer that can be melted and reshaped
The chains are held by weak forces
It can be recycled by melting
A plastic that softens on heating — chains held by weak intermolecular forces, so they can slide over each other when warm

definition: A polymer that does not soften when heated. Has cross-links between polymer chains that prevent them from sliding over each other.
clues: This is a type of polymer that does not melt when heated
It has cross-links between chains
It sets permanently and cannot be reshaped
A plastic with cross-links between polymer chains — these prevent softening, so it is used where heat resistance is needed

definition: A particle with dimensions between 1 and 100 nanometres. They have a very high surface area to volume ratio and different properties to the bulk material.
clues: This is a very small type of particle
It is between 1 and 100 nanometres in size
It has a high surface area to volume ratio
An extremely small particle — its huge surface area to volume ratio gives it different and enhanced properties

definition: A unit of length equal to one billionth of a metre (10⁻⁹ m). Used to measure atoms, molecules and nanoparticles.
clues: This is a unit of measurement for very small things
It equals one billionth of a metre
It is used to measure atoms and nanoparticles
10⁻⁹ metres — the unit used to measure atoms, molecules and the tiny scale of nanoparticles

definition: The ratio of the surface area of a particle to its volume. As particles get smaller, this ratio increases, making them more reactive.
clues: This is a ratio that changes with particle size
It increases as particles get smaller
It affects how reactive a substance is
As a particle shrinks, this ratio increases — nanoparticles have a far greater value than bulk material, enhancing reactivity

definition: A diagram showing the arrangement of electrons in bonds between atoms using dots (from one atom) and crosses (from the other).
clues: This is a type of diagram used in chemistry
It shows electrons as dots and crosses
It represents how atoms bond together
A diagram showing electron arrangement in bonding — dots represent electrons from one atom, crosses from the other

definition: Different structural forms of the same element. Carbon has several allotropes including diamond, graphite, graphene and fullerenes.
clues: This term applies when one element exists in multiple structural forms
Carbon has several examples
Diamond and graphite are examples of the same element in different forms
Different structural arrangements of the same element — e.g. carbon exists as diamond, graphite, graphene and fullerenes

definition: A giant covalent compound (SiO₂) where each silicon atom is bonded to four oxygen atoms. Very hard, high melting point. Found in sand and quartz.
clues: This is a giant covalent compound with formula SiO₂
Each silicon atom is bonded to four oxygen atoms
It is the main component of sand
A giant covalent lattice of silicon and oxygen atoms — very hard, extremely high melting point, found in quartz and sand

definition: The force of attraction between oppositely charged particles (e.g. positive ions and negative ions, or positive ions and delocalised electrons).
clues: This is a force between oppositely charged particles
It holds ionic compounds and metals together
It acts between positive and negative charges
The attractive force between opposite charges — the basis of ionic bonding and also of metallic bonding

definition: The property of metals that allows them to be hammered or rolled into sheets without breaking. Due to layers of ions being able to slide over each other.
clues: This is a property of metals
It means a material can be beaten into thin sheets
It is explained by the structure of metals
The ability of a metal to be shaped without fracturing — layers of ions can slide over each other within the metallic lattice

definition: A pair of electrons on an atom that is not involved in a covalent bond.
clues: This is a feature of some atoms in covalent compounds
It is not shared with any other atom
Water has two of them on its oxygen atom
A pair of electrons on an atom that takes no part in bonding — e.g. the two lone pairs on oxygen in a water molecule
